catalog_quote: 2.3 Tones in Baba I This section is aimed at acquainting the reader with the tone patterns and possible tonal phenomena attested in Baba I which is a tone language. Steven Bird (1999d) considers a tone language as one in which voice pitch on an individual syllable may carry either a lexically or grammatically contrastive meaning. Welmers (1959: 2) sees a tone language as one in which both pitch phonemes and segmental phonemes enter into the composition of at least some morphemes. This means that some morphemes may lack a pitch phoneme while others may be exclusively made up of a tone without any segmental components or tone bearing units. It is in line with the above view that our analysis of Baba I tonal system is based. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Baba 1 is described as a tone language with two underlying level tones (H, L) on each tone-bearing unit, plus derived contour tones, downstep and floating tones; the only full description of the language says nothing about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal detail only (contour tones limited to two tonemes per TBU and mostly phrase-derived; toneless grammatical morphemes acquire tone by spreading).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on morphemes/words in citation form; tone rules (docking, spreading, downstep) apply across word boundaries in associative and verb constructions. No stress domain stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Baba 1 (su papiax 'speech of the Baba 1 people'; Papia/Bapa/Bapakum, Ethnologue bbw), Ndop plain, Ngoketunjia Division, NW Cameroon = Glottolog baba1264; author is a native speaker. Explicitly distinct from Baba 2 (a Ngemba variety in Mezam Division).

sources.note: Ch.1 syllable/morpheme structure, ch.2 phonological processes + sec.2.3 'Tones in Baba I' (pp.52-61): Baba 1 'is a tone language', two underlying tones H and L, contour tones (max two tonemes per TBU), spreading, replacement, contour simplification, downstep, floating tones; ch.3 orthography marks tone. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the thesis (text-layer a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence and scanned variants: nil outside syntax chapters).
